claim: Eighteen subjects between 21 and 33 years of age (mean age 26.2; nine females) participated in the MEG experiment.
source: Eighteen subjects between 21 and 33 years of age (mean age 26.2; nine females) participated in the MEG experiment.
evidence: Direct statement about participant demographics in the MEG study

claim: Nineteen additional subjects (age range = 19–32; mean age = 24.6; 11 females) participated in a 7T fMRI experiment, using a similar task paradigm as in the MEG experiment.
source: Nineteen additional subjects (age range = 19–32; mean age = 24.6; 11 females) participated in a 7T fMRI experiment, using a similar task paradigm as in the MEG experiment (González-García et al., 2018).
evidence: Direct statement about participant demographics in the fMRI study with citation to previous work

claim: The two subject groups (MEG and fMRI) did not have any overlap since subjects needed to be naïve to the Mooney images used in this experiment.
source: The two subject groups did not have any overlap since subjects needed to be naïve to the Mooney images used in this experiment.
evidence: Direct statement about experimental design requirement

claim: Mooney images are degraded, two-tone images created from natural photographs of objects and animals.
source: These Mooney images are degraded, two-tone images created from natural photographs of objects and animals.
evidence: Direct description of stimulus properties

claim: The content of Mooney images typically remains unrecognizable even after multiple presentations.
source: Even after multiple presentations, the content of these images typically remains unrecognizable.
evidence: Statement about typical perceptual outcome with Mooney images

claim: Once exposed to the corresponding non-degraded original photograph, subjects effortlessly recognize the Mooney image in future presentations.
source: However, once exposed to the corresponding non-degraded original photograph, subjects effortlessly recognize the Mooney image in future presentations – a disambiguation effect that lasts for days, months, even a lifetime (Ludmer et al., 2011; Albright, 2012).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research

claim: The disambiguation effect with Mooney images lasts for days, months, even a lifetime.
source: However, once exposed to the corresponding non-degraded original photograph, subjects effortlessly recognize the Mooney image in future presentations – a disambiguation effect that lasts for days, months, even a lifetime (Ludmer et al., 2011; Albright, 2012).
evidence: Statement about duration of disambiguation effect supported by citations

claim: Disambiguation of Mooney images induces widespread activation in both visual and frontoparietal cortices.
source: Previous neuroimaging studies have observed that disambiguation of Mooney images induces widespread activation and enhanced image-specific information in both visual and frontoparietal cortices (Dolan et al., 1997; Hegdé and Kersten, 2010; Hsieh et al., 2010; Gorlin et al., 2012; van Loon et al., 2016; González-García et al., 2018).
evidence: Summary of previous neuroimaging findings with multiple citations

claim: Disambiguation of Mooney images induces enhanced image-specific information in both visual and frontoparietal cortices.
source: Previous neuroimaging studies have observed that disambiguation of Mooney images induces widespread activation and enhanced image-specific information in both visual and frontoparietal cortices (Dolan et al., 1997; Hegdé and Kersten, 2010; Hsieh et al., 2010; Gorlin et al., 2012; van Loon et al., 2016; González-García et al., 2018).
evidence: Summary of previous neuroimaging findings with multiple citations

claim: Recognition of Mooney images, even after disambiguation, is slow with reaction times at around 1.2 s.
source: This is an important open question because behavioral studies have shown that recognition of Mooney images, even after disambiguation, is slow – with reaction times at around 1.2 s (Hegdé and Kersten, 2010).
evidence: Statement about behavioral timing supported by citation

claim: Neural dynamics underlying recognition of intact, unambiguous images typically conclude within 500 ms.
source: By contrast, neural dynamics underlying recognition of intact, unambiguous images, as well as scene-facilitation of object recognition, typically conclude within 500 ms (Carlson et al., 2013; van de Nieuwenhuijzen et al., 2013; Kaiser et al., 2016; Brandman and Peelen, 2017).
evidence: Statement about timing of neural dynamics for unambiguous images supported by citations

claim: Neural dynamics underlying scene-facilitation of object recognition typically conclude within 500 ms.
source: By contrast, neural dynamics underlying recognition of intact, unambiguous images, as well as scene-facilitation of object recognition, typically conclude within 500 ms (Carlson et al., 2013; van de Nieuwenhuijzen et al., 2013; Kaiser et al., 2016; Brandman and Peelen, 2017).
evidence: Statement about timing of neural dynamics for scene-facilitated recognition supported by citations

claim: Previous EEG and MEG studies reported disambiguation-induced decrease in beta-band power.
source: Several previous EEG and MEG studies reported disambiguation-induced decrease in beta-band power and increase in gamma-band power (Grützner et al., 2010; Minami et al., 2014; Moratti et al., 2014), but these effects could potentially be attributed to non-content-specific effects such as increased attention, salience or decreased task difficulty following disambiguation.
evidence: Summary of previous EEG/MEG findings with citations

claim: Previous EEG and MEG studies reported disambiguation-induced increase in gamma-band power.
source: Several previous EEG and MEG studies reported disambiguation-induced decrease in beta-band power and increase in gamma-band power (Grützner et al., 2010; Minami et al., 2014; Moratti et al., 2014), but these effects could potentially be attributed to non-content-specific effects such as increased attention, salience or decreased task difficulty following disambiguation.
evidence: Summary of previous EEG/MEG findings with citations

claim: There was a significant main effect of presentation stage (pre- vs. post-disambiguation) on subjective recognition (F1,68 = 42.6, p=1.0 × 10−8, η2p = 0.38).
source: There was a significant main effect of presentation stage (pre- vs. post-disambiguation) on both subjective recognition (Figure 2A, left, F1,68 = 42.6, p=1.0 × 10−8, η2p = 0.38) and verbal identification (Figure 2A, right, F1,68 = 60.7, p=5.2 × 10−11, η2p = 0.47).
evidence: Statistical result from ANOVA analysis shown in Figure 2A

claim: There was a significant main effect of presentation stage (pre- vs. post-disambiguation) on verbal identification (F1,68 = 60.7, p=5.2 × 10−11, η2p = 0.47).
source: There was a significant main effect of presentation stage (pre- vs. post-disambiguation) on both subjective recognition (Figure 2A, left, F1,68 = 42.6, p=1.0 × 10−8, η2p = 0.38) and verbal identification (Figure 2A, right, F1,68 = 60.7, p=5.2 × 10−11, η2p = 0.47).
evidence: Statistical result from ANOVA analysis shown in Figure 2A

claim: There was a significant interaction effect of presentation stage × image set type on subjective recognition (F1,68 = 16.4, p=1.0 × 10−4, η2p = 0.19).
source: Crucially, there was also a significant interaction effect of presentation stage × image set type on both subjective recognition (F1,68 = 16.4, p=1.0 × 10−4, η2p = 0.19) and verbal identification (F1,68 = 38.5, p=3.7 × 10−8, η2p = 0.36), suggesting that the effect of disambiguation by viewing the corresponding grayscale image significantly exceeds that induced by repetition.
evidence: Statistical result from ANOVA analysis

claim: There was a significant interaction effect of presentation stage × image set type on verbal identification (F1,68 = 38.5, p=3.7 × 10−8, η2p = 0.36).
source: Crucially, there was also a significant interaction effect of presentation stage × image set type on both subjective recognition (F1,68 = 16.4, p=1.0 × 10−4, η2p = 0.19) and verbal identification (F1,68 = 38.5, p=3.7 × 10−8, η2p = 0.36), suggesting that the effect of disambiguation by viewing the corresponding grayscale image significantly exceeds that induced by repetition.
evidence: Statistical result from ANOVA analysis

claim: The effect of disambiguation by viewing the corresponding grayscale image significantly exceeds that induced by repetition.
source: Crucially, there was also a significant interaction effect of presentation stage × image set type on both subjective recognition (F1,68 = 16.4, p=1.0 × 10−4, η2p = 0.19) and verbal identification (F1,68 = 38.5, p=3.7 × 10−8, η2p = 0.36), suggesting that the effect of disambiguation by viewing the corresponding grayscale image significantly exceeds that induced by repetition.
evidence: Inference drawn from statistical interaction effect

claim: No main or interaction effect involving presentation number was significant (all p>0.2) in the three-way ANOVA on subjective recognition rates.
source: No main or interaction effect involving presentation number was significant (all p>0.2).
evidence: Statistical result from three-way ANOVA

claim: There was a highly significant interaction effect of presentation stage × image set type (F1,408 = 85.2, p=1.5 × 10−18, η2p = 0.17) in the three-way ANOVA on subjective recognition rates.
source: However, consistent with the previous analysis, there was a highly significant interaction effect of presentation stage ×image set type (F1,408 = 85.2, p=1.5 × 10−18, η2p = 0.17).
evidence: Statistical result from three-way ANOVA

claim: Viewing the corresponding grayscale image, but not repeated viewing of the Mooney image, significantly facilitates Mooney image recognition.
source: These results suggest that viewing the corresponding grayscale image, but not repeated viewing of the Mooney image, significantly facilitates Mooney image recognition.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the three-way ANOVA results

claim: For real image sets, 60.9 ± 4.2% are not recognized and 34.0 ± 3.4% are recognized in the pre-disambiguation stage.
source: Based on these criteria, for real image sets, 60.9 ± 4.2% are not recognized and 34.0 ± 3.4% are recognized in the pre-disambiguation stage, whereas only 10.3 ± 2.4% are not recognized and 87.4 ± 2.5% are recognized in the post-disambiguation stage.
evidence: Quantitative behavioral data from the experiment

claim: For real image sets, only 10.3 ± 2.4% are not recognized and 87.4 ± 2.5% are recognized in the post-disambiguation stage.
source: Based on these criteria, for real image sets, 60.9 ± 4.2% are not recognized and 34.0 ± 3.4% are recognized in the pre-disambiguation stage, whereas only 10.3 ± 2.4% are not recognized and 87.4 ± 2.5% are recognized in the post-disambiguation stage.
evidence: Quantitative behavioral data from the experiment

claim: Following the acquisition of perceptual priors, different degraded images are represented much more distinctly in neural dynamics starting from ~500 ms after stimulus onset.
source: We observed that following the acquisition of perceptual priors, different degraded images are represented much more distinctly in neural dynamics starting from ~500 ms after stimulus onset.
evidence: Summary statement of main MEG finding from the abstract

claim: Content-specific neural activity related to stimulus-feature processing dominated within 300 ms after stimulus onset.
source: Content-specific neural activity related to stimulus-feature processing dominated within 300 ms after stimulus onset, while content-specific neural activity related to recognition processing dominated from 500 ms onward.
evidence: Summary statement of main finding from the abstract

claim: Content-specific neural activity related to recognition processing dominated from 500 ms onward.
source: Content-specific neural activity related to stimulus-feature processing dominated within 300 ms after stimulus onset, while content-specific neural activity related to recognition processing dominated from 500 ms onward.
evidence: Summary statement of main finding from the abstract

claim: With SCP activity, the classifier using real image sets performed significantly above chance level at every time point from 300 ms onward (p<0.05, cluster-based permutation test).
source: With SCP activity (Figure 3A), the classifier using real image sets performed significantly above chance level at every time point from 300 ms onward (green trace and bar, p<0.05, cluster-based permutation test).
evidence: Statistical result from multivariate pattern decoding analysis shown in Figure 3A

claim: The classifier applied to catch image sets yielded chance-level accuracy throughout the trial epoch.
source: By contrast, the classifier applied to catch image sets yielded chance-level accuracy throughout the trial epoch (black).
evidence: Result from control analysis using catch images

claim: Decoding of presentation stage based on six randomly selected real image sets yielded sustained significant decoding from 300 ms onward.
source: A control analysis showed that decoding of presentation stage based on six randomly selected real image sets to match the statistical power of catch image sets still yielded sustained significant decoding from 300 ms onward (figure not shown).
evidence: Result from control analysis matching statistical power

claim: Activation patterns reveal strong frontotemporal contributions starting within 400 ms after stimulus onset.
source: Activation patterns corresponding to the SCP and ERF classifiers based on subjective recognition responses (Figure 3A–B, blue traces) are plotted in Figure 3C, which reveal strong frontotemporal contributions starting within 400 ms after stimulus onset (note that both large positive and large negative values contribute strongly to the classifier).
evidence: Result from activation pattern analysis shown in Figure 3C

claim: For the classifier trained at 400 ms, its cross-time generalization time course departs significantly from the within-time decoding time course (p<0.05, paired t-tests, FDR corrected).
source: For the classifier trained at 400 ms (bottom row), its cross-time generalization time course departs significantly from the within-time decoding time course (shown as shaded areas, p<0.05, paired t-tests, FDR corrected).
evidence: Statistical result from cross-time generalization analysis

claim: For the classifiers trained at 800 ms or later, their cross-time generalization accuracies closely tracked the within-time decoding accuracy.
source: By contrast, for the classifiers trained at 800 ms or later, their cross-time generalization accuracies closely tracked the within-time decoding accuracy.
evidence: Result from cross-time generalization analysis

claim: The results suggest evolving patterns of neural activity until ~800 ms after stimulus onset and thereafter sustained activity patterns that distinguish pre- and post-disambiguation perceptual states.
source: Together, these results suggest evolving patterns of neural activity until ~800 ms after stimulus onset and thereafter sustained activity patterns that distinguish pre- and post-disambiguation perceptual states.
evidence: Interpretation of cross-time generalization results

claim: From ~500 ms onward, across-image dissimilarity was substantially lower for pre-disambiguation Mooney images than for post-disambiguation Mooney images or grayscale images, and this difference is significant from ~1 s to the end of the trial epoch (p<0.05, cluster-based permutation tests).
source: However, from ~500 ms onward, across-image dissimilarity was substantially lower for pre-disambiguation Mooney images (gold) than for post-disambiguation Mooney images (teal) or grayscale images (black), and this difference is significant from ~1 s to the end of the trial epoch (p<0.05, cluster-based permutation tests).
evidence: Statistical result from RSA analysis of across-image dissimilarity

claim: The difference between post-disambiguation Mooney images and gray-images was not significant at any time point.
source: The difference between post-disambiguation Mooney images and gray-images was not significant at any time point.
evidence: Statistical result from RSA analysis

claim: A similar analysis applied to catch image sets did not yield any significant difference between pre- and post-disambiguation stages, or between Mooney and grayscale images.
source: A similar analysis applied to catch image sets did not yield any significant difference between pre- and post-disambiguation stages, or between Mooney and grayscale images (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Result from control analysis using catch images shown in supplementary figure

claim: Following the acquisition of perceptual priors, different Mooney images are represented much more distinctly in neural dynamics, in fact as distinctly as the grayscale images.
source: Together, these results suggest that, even though Mooney images presented in the two task stages are physically identical, following the acquisition of perceptual priors, different Mooney images are represented much more distinctly in neural dynamics, in fact as distinctly as the grayscale images.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from RSA results

claim: Pre-disambiguation Mooney images are well separable from their matching grayscale images from 50 ms until the end of trial epoch (p<0.05, cluster-based permutation test).
source: The result, plotted in Figure 5C–ii, shows that pre-disambiguation Mooney images are well separable from their matching grayscale images from 50 ms until the end of trial epoch (orange trace and significance bar, p<0.05, cluster-based permutation test).
evidence: Statistical result from single-trial separability analysis shown in Figure 5C

claim: Post-disambiguation Mooney images are separable from their matching grayscale images only in a short window – from 50 to 530 ms.
source: By contrast, post-disambiguation Mooney images are separable from their matching grayscale images only in a short window – from 50 to 530 ms (Figure 5C–ii, dark blue).
evidence: Result from single-trial separability analysis shown in Figure 5C

claim: Neural representation of a post-disambiguation image is entirely indistinguishable from that of its matching grayscale image from ~550 ms onward.
source: Strikingly, neural representation of a post-disambiguation image is entirely indistinguishable from that of its matching grayscale image from ~550 ms onward (as shown by separability fluctuating around chance level; Figure 5C–ii, dark blue), despite the difference in the stimulus input.
evidence: Result from single-trial separability analysis shown in Figure 5C

claim: The separability between the same Mooney image presented before and after disambiguation reaches significance at 270 ms, which remains significant until the end of trial epoch.
source: The separability between the same Mooney image presented before and after disambiguation starts to increase after stimulus onset, and reaches significance at 270 ms, which remains significant until the end of trial epoch (Figure 5C–ii, green).
evidence: Statistical result from single-trial separability analysis shown in Figure 5C

claim: Early (<300 ms) neural activity patterns distinguish between different physical stimulus inputs – Mooney vs. grayscale images.
source: These results suggest that early (<300 ms) neural activity patterns distinguish between different physical stimulus inputs – Mooney vs. grayscale images, while late (>500 ms) neural activity patterns distinguish between recognizing the image content and failing to do so.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from single-trial separability results

claim: Late (>500 ms) neural activity patterns distinguish between recognizing the image content and failing to do so.
source: These results suggest that early (<300 ms) neural activity patterns distinguish between different physical stimulus inputs – Mooney vs. grayscale images, while late (>500 ms) neural activity patterns distinguish between recognizing the image content and failing to do so.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from single-trial separability results

claim: Although neural activity patterns elicited by a post-disambiguation image are indistinguishable from those elicited by its matching grayscale image after 550 ms, they are well separable from other grayscale images.
source: The comparison between the Post-Gray traces in Figure 5C–ii and Figure 5D–ii (dark blue) reveals a striking effect after 550 ms: although neural activity patterns elicited by a post-disambiguation image are indistinguishable from those elicited by its matching grayscale image, they are well separable from other grayscale images, suggesting an image-specific shift in neural representation toward the relevant prior experience that guides perception.
evidence: Result from comparing diagonal and off-diagonal separability shown in Figures 5C and 5D

claim: There is an image-specific shift in neural representation toward the relevant prior experience that guides perception.
source: The comparison between the Post-Gray traces in Figure 5C–ii and Figure 5D–ii (dark blue) reveals a striking effect after 550 ms: although neural activity patterns elicited by a post-disambiguation image are indistinguishable from those elicited by its matching grayscale image, they are well separable from other grayscale images, suggesting an image-specific shift in neural representation toward the relevant prior experience that guides perception.
evidence: Inference drawn from separability analysis results

claim: Early (<300 ms) neural dynamics carry stimulus-content-specific processing and late (>500 ms) neural dynamics carry recognition-content-specific processing.
source: Together, these results provide strong evidence that early (<300 ms) neural dynamics carry stimulus-content-specific processing and late (>500 ms) neural dynamics carry recognition-content-specific processing.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple separability analyses

claim: Neural activity reflecting stimulus processing exhibited an early sharp peak reaching significance at 30–310 ms following stimulus onset.
source: Neural activity reflecting stimulus processing (indexed by r[Pre-Pre,Post-Post]) exhibited an early sharp peak reaching significance at 30–310 ms following stimulus onset and a small second peak that reaches significance at 1340–1420 ms (p<0.05, cluster-based permutation test; Figure 4E, green).
evidence: Statistical result from intra-RDM analysis shown in Figure 4E

claim: Neural activity reflecting stimulus processing exhibited a small second peak that reaches significance at 1340–1420 ms.
source: Neural activity reflecting stimulus processing (indexed by r[Pre-Pre,Post-Post]) exhibited an early sharp peak reaching significance at 30–310 ms following stimulus onset and a small second peak that reaches significance at 1340–1420 ms (p<0.05, cluster-based permutation test; Figure 4E, green).
evidence: Statistical result from intra-RDM analysis shown in Figure 4E

claim: Neural activity reflecting recognition processing reaches significance at 690–1240 ms and again from 1550 ms to after stimulus offset.
source: By contrast, neural activity reflecting recognition processing (indexed by r[Post-Post,Gray-Gray]) occurs in a broad temporal period: it onsets shortly after stimulus onset and reaches significance at 690–1240 ms and again from 1550 ms to after stimulus offset (Figure 4E, magenta).
evidence: Statistical result from intra-RDM analysis shown in Figure 4E

claim: The correlation between Pre-Pre and Gray-Gray squares of the RDM was not significant at any time point.
source: As a control measure, the correlation between Pre-Pre and Gray-Gray squares of the RDM was not significant at any time point, suggesting that, as expected, representational geometry is different between conditions with different stimulus input and different recognition outcomes.
evidence: Result from control analysis in intra-RDM analysis

claim: The stimulus model dominates in the early period before 500 ms and exhibits a second broad plateau between 600 ms and 2.5 s, reaching statistical significance at 50–410 and 620–2410 ms (p<0.05, cluster-based permutation test).
source: The results reveal distinct temporal waveforms for neural activity related to each model (Figure 6D): the stimulus model dominates in the early period before 500 ms and exhibits a second broad plateau between 600 ms and 2.5 s, reaching statistical significance at 50–410 and 620–2410 ms (p<0.05, cluster-based permutation test).
evidence: Statistical result from model-based RSA shown in Figure 6D

claim: The recognition model dominates in the late period, from ~500 ms to 2.5 s, reaching significance from 670 ms until the end of trial epoch.
source: By contrast, the recognition model dominates in the late period, from ~500 ms to 2.5 s, reaching significance from 670 ms until the end of trial epoch.
evidence: Statistical result from model-based RSA

claim: The attention model shows a peak at the transition between stimulus and recognition models, around 500 ms after stimulus onset, and reaches significance at 400–570 ms.
source: Interestingly, the attention model shows a peak at the transition between stimulus and recognition models, around 500 ms after stimulus onset, and reaches significance at 400–570 ms.
evidence: Statistical result from model-based RSA

claim: The stimulus-related effects had the earliest onset in the right V1 and V2 at 80 ms, followed by progressive recruitment of areas along the visual hierarchy.
source: The stimulus-related effects (Figure 6E–i) had the earliest onset in the right V1 and V2 at 80 ms, followed by progressive recruitment of areas along the visual hierarchy.
evidence: Result from MEG-fMRI fusion analysis shown in Figure 6E

claim: Stimulus-related effects in bilateral frontal cortices reached significance at 230 ms (right) and 240 ms (left).
source: Stimulus-related effects in most higher order frontoparietal regions reached significance much later (after 400 ms), with the exception of bilateral frontal cortices (right: 230 ms; left: 240 ms) and the PCC (240 ms), where significant effects occurred nearly simultaneously with the last visual areas.
evidence: Result from MEG-fMRI fusion analysis

claim: Stimulus-related effects in the PCC reached significance at 240 ms.
source: Stimulus-related effects in most higher order frontoparietal regions reached significance much later (after 400 ms), with the exception of bilateral frontal cortices (right: 230 ms; left: 240 ms) and the PCC (240 ms), where significant effects occurred nearly simultaneously with the last visual areas.
evidence: Result from MEG-fMRI fusion analysis

claim: After 600 ms, stimulus-related effects exhibit sustained significance across category-selective visual areas (LOC and FG) and frontoparietal regions (FPN and DMN), and recurrent transient significance in early visual areas (V1-V4).
source: Interestingly, after 600 ms, stimulus-related effects exhibit sustained significance across category-selective visual areas (LOC and FG) and frontoparietal regions (FPN and DMN), and, at the same time, recurrent transient significance in early visual areas (V1-V4).
evidence: Result from MEG-fMRI fusion analysis

claim: The recognition-related effects exhibited broad spatiotemporal significance from ~650 ms until the end of trial epoch, covering all ROIs investigated but with earlier onset and more sustained significance in higher-order regions (LOC, FG, FPN and DMN) than early visual areas.
source: By contrast, the recognition-related effects (Figure 6E–ii) exhibited broad spatiotemporal significance from ~650 ms until the end of trial epoch, covering all ROIs investigated but with earlier onset and more sustained significance in higher-order regions (LOC, FG, FPN and DMN) than early visual areas.
evidence: Result from MEG-fMRI fusion analysis shown in Figure 6E

claim: Attention-related effects were only found in bilateral frontal and parietal cortices, which reached significance first in frontal cortices at 340 ms.
source: Attention-related effects were only found in bilateral frontal and parietal cortices, which reached significance first in frontal cortices at 340 ms (Figure 6E–iii).
evidence: Result from MEG-fMRI fusion analysis shown in Figure 6E

claim: Stimulus-feature processing progresses from lower to higher order brain regions in an early time window.
source: Importantly, they show that stimulus-feature processing progresses from lower to higher order brain regions in an early time window, while recognition-related processing proceeds from higher to lower order regions in a later time period.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from MEG-fMRI fusion results

claim: Recognition-related processing proceeds from higher to lower order regions in a later time period.
source: Importantly, they show that stimulus-feature processing progresses from lower to higher order brain regions in an early time window, while recognition-related processing proceeds from higher to lower order regions in a later time period.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from MEG-fMRI fusion results

claim: Attention-related processing mediated by frontoparietal regions occurs at an intermediate time latency (~500 ms) and may facilitate the transition from stimulus processing to successful recognition.
source: Moreover, attention-related processing mediated by frontoparietal regions occurs at an intermediate time latency (~500 ms) and may facilitate the transition from stimulus processing to successful recognition.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from MEG-fMRI fusion results with speculative interpretation

claim: Slow cortical potentials (<5 Hz) accounted for much of the perceptual state decoding effect.
source: Consistent with an earlier study (Baria et al., 2017), slow cortical potentials (<5 Hz) accounted for much of this effect.
evidence: Statement about frequency band contribution with citation to previous work

claim: The late recognition-related neural dynamics observed are consistent with human subjects' reaction times reporting recognition status for disambiguated Mooney images at around 1.2 s.
source: Yet, the late recognition-related neural dynamics observed herein are consistent with human subjects' reaction times reporting recognition status for disambiguated Mooney images at around 1.2 s (Hegdé and Kersten, 2010).
evidence: Comparison of current findings with previous behavioral results

claim: The latency related to recognition observed in the current study is substantially later than previously reported onset times of object category and face identity-related information.
source: We note that the latency related to recognition observed in the current study is substantially later than previously reported onset times of object category and face identity-related information (Carlson et al., 2013; van de Nieuwenhuijzen et al., 2013; Kaiser et al., 2016; Vida et al., 2017).
evidence: Comparison of current findings with previous studies

claim: Bottom-up stimulus information is ambiguous and much weaker for Mooney images than images showing clear and isolated objects typically used in object categorization tasks.
source: Several aspects likely contribute to this difference: first, bottom-up stimulus information is ambiguous and much weaker for Mooney images than images showing clear and isolated objects typically used in object categorization tasks
evidence: Explanation for differences in timing compared to previous studies

claim: Neural activity differentiating between object categories may also reflect early processing of low-level image features that differ between categories.
source: third, neural activity differentiating between object categories may also reflect early processing of low-level image features that differ between categories (Coggan et al., 2016).
evidence: Explanation for differences with citation to previous work

claim: Recruitment of perceptual templates encoded in higher order frontoparietal areas and long-distance recurrent activity are needed for prior-experience-guided visual ambiguity resolution.
source: Importantly, the present finding of slow neural dynamics underlying recognition-related processing is consistent with our hypothesis that recruitment of perceptual templates encoded in higher order frontoparietal areas and long-distance recurrent activity are needed for prior-experience-guided visual ambiguity resolution.
evidence: Hypothesis supported by the current findings

claim: Bilateral frontal cortices of the FPN are the only regions showing both attention-related activity and early stimulus-related activity that reaches significance at 230–240 ms.
source: We note that bilateral frontal cortices of the FPN are the only regions showing both attention-related activity and early stimulus-related activity that reaches significance at 230–240 ms – immediately following fusiform gyri at 220–230 ms.
evidence: Result from MEG-fMRI fusion analysis

claim: Following disambiguation, frontal areas of the FPN move up the cortical hierarchy as defined by the neural representation format.
source: This result resonates with our previous fMRI observation that following disambiguation, frontal areas of the FPN move up the cortical hierarchy as defined by the neural representation format (González-García et al., 2018).
evidence: Reference to previous fMRI finding

claim: Frontal areas may play a special role in utilizing internal priors to guide perceptual processing.
source: Together, these findings support the idea that frontal areas may play a special role in utilizing internal priors to guide perceptual processing (Bar et al., 2006; Summerfield et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: Interpretation supported by current findings and previous literature

claim: Behavioral and neural abnormalities associated with Mooney image disambiguation have been reported in patients with schizophrenia and autism.
source: In line with theories positing aberrant interactions between internal priors and sensory input in psychiatric illnesses (Friston et al., 2014), behavioral and neural abnormalities associated with Mooney image disambiguation have been reported in patients with schizophrenia and autism (Sun et al., 2012; Rivolta et al., 2014; Teufel et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement about clinical findings with citations

claim: Thirty-nine images (19 were inanimate objects, and 20 were animals) were chosen to be used in this experiment via an initial screening procedure.
source: From an original set of 252 images, thirty-nine (19 were inanimate objects, and 20 were animals – unbeknownst to the subjects) were chosen to be used in this experiment via an initial screening procedure conducted by six additional participants recruited separately from the main experiment [for details, see (Chang et al., 2016).
evidence: Description of stimulus selection procedure

claim: Of the 39 unique Mooney images used for the main experiment, 33 had their corresponding grayscale images presented ('real image sets'), while the remaining six were presented with non-matching grayscale images ('catch image sets') as controls.
source: Of the 39 unique Mooney images used for the main experiment, 33 had their corresponding grayscale images presented ('real image sets'), while the remaining six were presented with non-matching grayscale images ('catch image sets') as controls.
evidence: Description of experimental design

claim: Each unique grayscale image was presented three times for each subject.
source: In all, each unique grayscale image was presented three times for each subject, and each unique Mooney image was presented six times before and six times after disambiguation.
evidence: Description of experimental design

claim: Each unique Mooney image was presented six times before and six times after disambiguation.
source: In all, each unique grayscale image was presented three times for each subject, and each unique Mooney image was presented six times before and six times after disambiguation.
evidence: Description of experimental design

claim: MEG data were collected with a 600 Hz sampling rate and an anti-aliasing filter of 150 Hz.
source: MEG data were collected with a 600 Hz sampling rate and an anti-aliasing filter of 150 Hz.
evidence: Description of data acquisition parameters

claim: MEG data were filtered in two different frequency bands for further analyses: slow cortical potentials (SCPs, 0.05 – 5 Hz; down-sampled to 10 Hz), and classic event-related field (ERF) frequency range (DC – 35 Hz; down-sampled to 100 Hz).
source: MEG data were demeaned, detrended, and filtered in two different frequency bands (using 3rd-order Butterworth filters) for further analyses: slow cortical potentials (SCPs, 0.05 – 5 Hz; down-sampled to 10 Hz), and classic event-related field (ERF) frequency range (DC – 35 Hz; down-sampled to 100 Hz).
